meta.title: Black Book: Micro-Expressions
meta.subtitle: Reading Discomfort Before the Mask Goes Back On
meta.description: A field guide to the involuntary signals the face sends in under half a second. How to spot them, what they mean, what they don't mean, and how to use the read without getting it wrong.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: Watch for the Flash That Lasts Under Half a Second
cards.hook: A woman smiled at her doctors and asked to go home. One frame before the smile, her face flashed anguish. The doctors missed it. She had planned to use the weekend pass to end her life.
cards.truth:
The amygdala fires emotion before the conscious mind can stop the face.
• The real feeling leaks in under 1/12 of a second, then the mask goes back on.
• Most observers only see the mask — you need to catch the transition frame.
• Miss that frame and you will trust the performance instead of the person.
cards.remember: The face shows the real feeling once, then hides it.
cards.theySee: A person with a steady smile sitting across from them and speaking calmly while being asked questions.

signals.t: The face tightens for a single frame, then relaxes to baseline in under a second.
The mouth moves into a smile but the eyes stay flat for a beat before following.
Brows pull briefly downward before lifting back to a neutral position.
The corners of the lips press or pull tight for one frame, then release.

steps.title: Slow your scan
steps.desc: Stop watching for large reactions. Set your attention on movements under one second in the upper face only.

steps.title: Watch the transition
steps.desc: The leak happens as the face shifts from one expression to the next — focus on the frame before the held expression settles.

steps.title: Re-ask after a flash
steps.desc: When you catch something, ask the same question from a different angle. If the flash comes again on the same topic, it is real.

cards.script: "Let me come at that from a different angle — what part of this worries you most?"
cards.counter:
Someone trained to watch you runs the same scan in reverse.
• They watch the transition between expressions, not the held expression you are managing.
• If someone re-asks a question you answered smoothly, they caught something the first time.
• Don't rush to neutral — a fast cover-up is more visible than a brief honest reaction.
cards.insight: Catching the flash is straightforward once you know where to look. Getting the person to tell you what it meant — without tipping them off that you caught it — is the next problem.

cards.title: Look at the Eyes and Brows Before You Look at the Mouth
cards.hook: We learn to smile on command before age five. Nobody practices controlling their brows. That is where the honest data lives.
cards.truth:
The mouth is the most practiced part of the face. The upper face is not.
• Eyebrows move with emotion before a person can intercept them consciously.
• A fake smile reaches the mouth first and rarely reaches the eyes.
• The real signal almost always leaks from brow tension or eye-squint before anything else.
cards.remember: The mouth fakes it easily. The brows rarely do.
cards.theySee: A person smiling at them from across a table while their upper face stays flat and still.

signals.t: The mouth is smiling but the brows do not rise or soften with the expression.
There are no crow's feet lines around the eyes — the smile is mouth-only.
The inner brows drop briefly and pull together before the face resets to neutral.
A momentary squint appears around the eyes on a specific word or topic and vanishes.

steps.title: Block the mouth mentally
steps.desc: In your next conversation, focus only on the area from the nose upward for two full minutes. Ignore the mouth entirely.

steps.title: Watch brows during their answers
steps.desc: Track eyebrow movement specifically when the person is answering a charged question, not when they are asking one.

steps.title: Check for crow's feet
steps.desc: When someone smiles, look for lines around the outer eyes. No lines usually means the smile is performed, not felt.

cards.script: "You said you're fine with it — your face moved differently when you said that. What's the actual concern?"
cards.counter:
When you are covering discomfort, you likely control your mouth first and forget your brows.
• A person looking above your smile is reading your upper face, not your words.
• Before an important meeting, consciously loosen the muscles between your brows.
• If you feel tension around your eyes during a conversation, your face is already saying something.
cards.insight: Most people spend years holding a neutral expression around the mouth and zero time on their brows. That gap stays open by default — and it is the first place a trained reader goes.

cards.title: Catch the Gap Between What They Say and What Their Face Does
cards.hook: A colleague says "I'm totally fine with this." One corner of their lip pulls up for half a second. That is contempt. They are not fine with this at all.
cards.truth:
When words and face disagree, the face holds the real data.
• The face fires before the person can align it with the words they are saying.
• The mismatch — not each signal alone — is the strongest tell in the conversation.
• Probe on the mismatch. The person will confirm it or start talking more than they intended.
cards.remember: Words and face tell two different stories. Believe the face.
cards.theySee: A person saying yes and nodding while one lip corner lifts briefly on one side.

signals.t: The head nods yes while the brows drop slightly — agreement on the surface, doubt underneath.
They say a positive word while one lip corner lifts briefly in a one-sided expression.
Their voice stays even but the face tightens for a moment on a specific word.
An expression appears and disappears in under a second right after they finish a sentence.

steps.title: Watch the face during their answer
steps.desc: Look at their face while they are speaking — not before or after. The mismatch fires during the words, not in the silence.

steps.title: Find the specific word
steps.desc: When you catch a mismatch, replay the sentence mentally. Which exact word triggered the expression? That word is what you probe next.

steps.title: Name the emotion, not the behavior
steps.desc: Don't say "your face did something." Say: "Something about that point seems like it's not sitting right — what is it?"

cards.script: "You said yes, but something shifted on your face when you said it. What's the part you're not saying?"
cards.counter:
If someone names your expression while you are speaking, they caught a mismatch.
• Notice when you nod while feeling the opposite — your face already communicated the truth.
• Don't rush to smooth it over — a fast correction looks more suspicious than a brief pause.
• Whoever catches your mismatch first has the information advantage for the rest of the conversation.
cards.insight: The mismatch works in both directions. The more fluently you read it on others, the more exposed your own face becomes to anyone running the same scan across the table.

cards.title: Spot Disgust by the Nose Wrinkle and Raised Upper Lip Together
cards.hook: The nose wrinkle evolved to block bad smells. Now it fires at bad ideas too. And it shows up before the person knows they are doing it.
cards.truth:
Disgust is the strongest negative social signal and one of the hardest to fake away.
• The nose wrinkles and the upper lip lifts together — this takes under a quarter of a second.
• Telling yourself not to feel disgust while thinking about it makes you feel it more, not less.
• Disgust has three times more negative effect on attraction than fear does.
cards.remember: Disgust means they want out of this conversation.
cards.theySee: A person whose nose briefly wrinkles and upper lip rises when a specific idea is mentioned.

signals.t: The nose pulls upward and wrinkles briefly on a specific word or topic.
The upper lip rises slightly on one or both sides at the same moment as the nose wrinkle.
The head moves very slightly backward as if creating distance from something unpleasant.
After the nose-lip movement, a small frown settles briefly before the face resets.

steps.title: Watch the nose-to-lip zone
steps.desc: When you say something new — a price, a name, a plan — watch the area between the nose and upper lip for under a second.

steps.title: Find the trigger word
steps.desc: If you catch the signal, note which word or phrase was in the air when it fired. That is the specific thing they found unpleasant.

steps.title: Circle back with a direct question
steps.desc: Return to the trigger word: "What's your read on [that specific thing]?" Don't assume — confirm before you act on the signal.

cards.script: "Something I just said landed wrong — which part?"
cards.counter:
Trying to suppress disgust pulls your mind harder toward the disgusting thing.
• If you feel it, your nose will move before you can stop it.
• Reframe what you find unpleasant before the meeting starts, not while it is happening.
• If someone spots your disgust, clarify the target — disgust at an idea and disgust at a person look identical.
cards.insight: Disgust at an idea is treated the same as disgust at a person by everyone in the room. The person showing it usually thinks the difference is obvious. It is not.

cards.title: Read Fear From Wide Eyes and Raised Brows Happening at the Same Time
cards.hook: Wide eyes and raised brows can mean "I didn't see that coming" or "this is a threat." The face is the same both times. Only the situation tells you which one is happening.
cards.truth:
Fear shows as wide eyes, raised brows, and sometimes an open mouth — all at once.
• In a high-stress context, that combination signals real anxiety about what comes next.
• A negotiator who sees fear should give more information, not more pressure.
• In a low-stakes or playful context, the same face is likely surprise — context changes the read entirely.
cards.remember: Fear and surprise look the same. Only context tells them apart.
cards.theySee: A person whose eyes widen and brows lift the moment a specific number is put on the table.

signals.t: The eyes open wider than their baseline at a specific point in the conversation.
Both brows raise simultaneously and stay raised briefly before resetting.
The jaw drops slightly, creating a small opening that holds for a moment.
The torso or head moves slightly backward right as the expression appears.

steps.title: Note what topic triggered it
steps.desc: When you see the wide-eyes-plus-brows combination, freeze the moment mentally. What specific thing was just said or shown?

steps.title: Give more information on that topic
steps.desc: Don't push forward. Go back to the trigger topic and add detail — cost breakdown, timeline, proof — whatever applies to the moment.

steps.title: Watch if the expression resolves
steps.desc: If more information makes the wide-eyes soften back to baseline, it was fear of the unknown. If it doesn't, there is a deeper objection to find.

cards.script: "I want to make sure you have everything you need on that point — what would help you feel more confident here?"
cards.counter:
Fear on your face in a negotiation tells the other side exactly where your room to move ends.
• Wide eyes after a number lands signals that the number surprised you.
• Hold your face and breathe before reacting to a price or deadline.
• A trained reader will push harder or probe deeper right after catching your fear flash.
cards.insight: Fear is the one expression most useful to the other side when they catch it. It maps your limits more precisely than anything you would say out loud.

cards.title: Confirm Anger Only When All Three Face Zones Fire Together
cards.hook: Pressed lips alone is tension. Lowered brows alone is concentration. Both plus a hard stare is anger, and you need to change what you are doing right now.
cards.truth:
Anger requires all three facial zones engaged before you can confirm it.
• Zone one: brows lower and pull together, vertical lines appear between them.
• Zone two: eyes go hard or bulge; lips press firm or pull into a square shape.
• One zone alone could be fatigue, concentration, or bright light — wait for all three.
cards.remember: One signal is noise. All three zones firing is a problem.
cards.theySee: A person whose brows have pulled down, jaw is set, and eyes are fixed in a hard, unblinking stare.

signals.t: Both brows lower and pull toward the center, creating vertical creases between them.
One or more vertical lines appear between the eyebrows and hold there.
The lips press firmly together, with corners pulled down or into a tight shape.
The eyes fix on the target and hold, unblinking or close to it, without looking away.

steps.title: Wait for all three zones
steps.desc: Before deciding someone is angry, check: are the brows down, is the mouth set, and are the eyes hard? All three must be active before you act on the read.

steps.title: De-escalate before naming it
steps.desc: Say: "Let's slow down — I want to make sure I'm hearing you correctly." This gives them room without calling out their expression.

steps.title: Give a face-saving way out
steps.desc: Offer a reframe, a question, or a small concession that lets them shift expression without having to explain the anger. Don't corner them.

cards.script: "Let's slow down here — I want to make sure I'm hearing you correctly on this."
cards.counter:
If someone de-escalates right when your face tightens, they read your anger before you said a word.
• One zone firing alone is not anger — don't react as if you have been caught.
• If all three zones fired, you have already communicated hostility without intending to.
• Ask for a short break before continuing — it is the fastest way to reset what your face already said.
cards.insight: The three-zone rule cuts false positives. The harder move is knowing what to do with confirmed anger in the next thirty seconds — before it becomes a conversation about the anger itself.

cards.title: One-Sided Lip Pull Means They Feel Superior, Not That They Are Lying
cards.hook: One corner of the lip pulls up and holds there. That is contempt — the only one-sided emotion expression. Most people read it as a lie tell. They are wrong.
cards.truth:
Contempt signals rank and has no reliable connection to deception.
• It appears in innocent people questioned by someone they see as less capable.
• The same lip pull shows in people who feel their statement is being challenged unfairly.
• Reading it as deception will make you wrong. Reading it as a status signal will make you right.
cards.remember: Contempt signals rank, not deception. Even honest people show it.
cards.theySee: A person with one lip corner lifted and held, sitting still while being questioned or challenged.

signals.t: One lip corner lifts and holds while the other stays at rest — the expression is asymmetric.
The head moves very slightly backward, adding distance and an implied look-down angle.
The brows are not furrowed or raised — the face is otherwise neutral, only the lip moves.
The eyes hold contact without blinking more than normal — the look is flat and held.

steps.title: Identify the status gap
steps.desc: Ask yourself: does this person think they outrank me here — by title, expertise, or experience? If yes, contempt is the likely read, not dishonesty.

steps.title: Give them the expert position
steps.desc: Ask a question that puts them in the lead: "How would you handle this part?" This closes the status gap without naming it.

steps.title: Probe the specific trigger
steps.desc: Find what caused the contempt — a word, a claim, a credential — and address that specific thing. Don't address the contempt expression itself.

cards.script: "Walk me through how you'd handle this — I want to make sure I'm giving you enough room here."
cards.counter:
If someone treats your contempt as a lie tell, they will push harder than the situation calls for.
• If you feel superior in a conversation, your face has already communicated it.
• A one-sided lip pull in front of a trained reader puts you at a disadvantage immediately.
• Keep your face neutral when you feel superior — especially in formal or high-stakes settings.
cards.insight: Contempt is the only expression that gets worse when you try to explain it away. The move after catching it is to close the status gap — not to call out the expression.

cards.title: A Discomfort Signal Means Something Bothers Them, Not That They Are Lying
cards.hook: Innocent people get nervous when questioned. Nervous looks like guilty to most observers. Acting on that read has put innocent people in prison.
cards.truth:
Every discomfort signal tells you something is bothering a person — nothing more.
• They may be nervous, afraid of being misread, or genuinely troubled by the question itself.
• No single behavior — or combination of behaviors — proves deception. None. Not one.
• Treating discomfort as deception is an error with serious real-world consequences.
cards.remember: A discomfort signal means something is wrong, not that they lied.
cards.theySee: A nervous person sitting across from a questioner who leans forward and keeps pushing the same question harder.

signals.t: The face stiffens noticeably on a specific topic but relaxes when the topic changes.
They swallow more than once in quick succession while speaking or just after answering.
A hand moves to the face — nose, mouth, or chin — right after they finish answering.
Eye contact breaks briefly right after answering a specific question, then returns.

steps.title: Separate the signal from the conclusion
steps.desc: Write down what you observed specifically — a nose wrinkle, a swallow, a look away. Don't add a cause yet. Keep observation and conclusion on separate lines.

steps.title: Ask what is bothering them
steps.desc: Say directly: "Something about that question seemed uncomfortable — what's behind that for you?" Let them name the cause before you decide what it means.

steps.title: Let them explain before deciding
steps.desc: Listen to the explanation. Discomfort about being misread looks identical to discomfort about being caught. Only the explanation separates them.

cards.script: "Something about that question seems uncomfortable — what's behind that for you?"
cards.counter:
If someone uses your discomfort face as evidence that you are lying, name the error.
• Say: "Being questioned makes me uncomfortable. That doesn't make me dishonest."
• Ask what specific behavior led to their conclusion — vague accusations are easier to address than specific ones.
• The more nervous you act about being read, the more you confirm their wrong conclusion.
cards.insight: The same training that lets you read discomfort also makes you more likely to read it as deception. The gap between "something is wrong" and "they are lying" is where most readers — and most verdicts — go wrong.

cards.title: The Feet Tell You More Than the Face Does
cards.hook: Over 215 body behaviors signal psychological discomfort. Most are not on the face. The feet are the most honest part of the body because nobody trained them to lie.
cards.truth:
The face is the most practiced part of a person's body. The feet are the least.
• Feet point toward what a person wants to move toward — and away from what they want to leave.
• Training only on the face misses the majority of discomfort data the body sends.
• A person can hold a neutral face while their feet have already left the conversation.
cards.remember: Most people manage their face. Almost nobody manages their feet.
cards.theySee: A person with a calm, neutral face sitting across from them while both feet point toward the nearest exit.

signals.t: One or both feet turn away from the conversation partner and toward an exit or open space.
A knee or foot bounces repeatedly at a faster rate when a specific topic comes up.
The torso moves backward in the chair or while standing, increasing physical distance.
A foot taps the floor once or twice right as a specific word or question is raised.

steps.title: Drop your gaze below the table
steps.desc: In your next sitting conversation, spend thirty seconds looking at feet and legs when you can do so without being noticed.

steps.title: Track foot direction by topic
steps.desc: Note which way feet are pointing when specific topics come up. If they shift direction on a certain subject, that subject is the one to probe.

steps.title: Compare face and feet
steps.desc: When the face looks calm but the feet are moving or turned away, believe the feet. Write a note immediately after the meeting on what topic triggered the split.

cards.script: "Before we move on — you seem like you want to get off this topic. What's the part that's not working?"
cards.counter:
If someone reads your feet, your face was already managed too well for them to use it.
• Place your feet flat on the floor before high-stakes conversations — it limits unintended signals.
• Notice when your own foot tap or leg bounce starts — it tells you which topic is hitting a nerve.
• The person watching below the table has a data channel you haven't thought to close.
cards.insight: The feet are honest because nobody told you to train them. This card closes that window — the moment you know the read, you become harder to read that way. Everyone else stays open.

cards.title: Read the Situation Before You Read the Face
cards.hook: Wide eyes and raised brows can mean "I'm scared" or "I didn't see that coming." The face is identical both times. Only the situation tells you which one is happening.
cards.truth:
Every expression carries different weight depending on what is happening around it.
• Fear in a job interview and the same face during a game mean entirely different things.
• Culture, the existing relationship, and the power gap all change what a signal means.
• Getting the context wrong makes your read worse than having no read at all.
cards.principle: Reid: Contextual Interpretation of Nonverbal Signals
cards.remember: The same face means different things in different situations.
cards.theySee: A person showing what looks like fear when the news they just heard was actually good and surprising.

signals.t: The face shows strong emotion but the content of the conversation doesn't warrant it — the baseline was already off.
The expression stays on the face for three or more seconds — longer than a micro-expression, possibly performed.
Their face was already tight or animated before the charged topic came up — the room, not the topic, is the cause.
The person is from a background where this expression carries a different social meaning than the observer assumes.

steps.title: Set a baseline first
steps.desc: Before the charged topic comes up, ask a neutral question and watch the face. That is the baseline. Only read against that — not against your assumption of normal.

steps.title: Check the stress level in the room
steps.desc: If the room is already tense before you start, faces will show more emotion across the board. Discount all readings by the pressure already present.

steps.title: Compare neutral and charged topics back to back
steps.desc: Ask one neutral question then one charged question immediately after. The difference in face between the two is the real signal — not either face alone.

cards.script: "Tell me what you walked in thinking today — before we got into any of this."
cards.counter:
Context is where most readers make their worst mistakes, and those mistakes are hard to call out without evidence.
• If someone misreads your face, name the context: "I look like that when I'm thinking, not when I'm worried."
• Give the reader the missing context before they draw the wrong conclusion.
• The more context you share voluntarily, the harder it is for someone to build a false read on your signals.
cards.insight: The best readers are not better at reading faces. They are better at reading situations. The face just confirms what the situation already told them. Get the situation wrong and the face means nothing.

cards.title: Telling Someone to Hide Disgust Makes Them Feel It More
cards.hook: People told to suppress disgust while watching something unpleasant thought about the disgusting thing more — and felt worse overall. Suppression is not control. It makes the feeling louder.
cards.truth:
Trying not to show an emotion pulls more mental energy toward that emotion.
• The person who thinks "don't react" reacts more, not less — the conscious effort backfires.
• The face leaks harder under suppression because the effort is conscious, not at the muscle level.
• The correct move is to change what you are thinking about, not how you are expressing it.
cards.remember: Fighting an emotion you don't want to show makes it louder.
cards.theySee: A person holding their face very still while tension shows around their eyes and mouth.

signals.t: The face looks controlled but there is visible tension around the eyes or mouth that does not belong in a relaxed expression.
The mouth is held unnaturally fixed — not relaxed, but not expressing anything either.
They wait too long before responding — the delay is longer than thought requires.
A suppressed expression holds briefly, then releases in a bigger version of itself a moment later.

steps.title: Replace the thought, not the expression
steps.desc: Before a hard conversation, pick one neutral fact about the person or situation to focus on. Think about that instead of what bothers you.

steps.title: Let small expressions go
steps.desc: In the conversation, let minor expressions pass without chasing them back to neutral. Stopping them pulls you harder into the feeling you are trying to leave.

steps.title: Take a beat out loud
steps.desc: If a strong feeling hits in the moment, say "Give me a second" and pause. This is visible and normal. Fighting it invisibly is what gives it away.

cards.script: "I'm going to take a second before I respond to that."
cards.counter:
If you notice someone trying not to react, they are reacting. The strain is the signal.
• Watch for over-controlled faces — mouth too still, brows fighting each other.
• A person who pauses too long before reacting is managing something the first frame already showed.
• When suppression is obvious, probe gently — they already told you something is there.
cards.insight: The correct answer to an emotion you can't show is not to suppress it. It is to decide what to think about instead. Most people never figure that out — which is why the suppression signal is one of the most reliable tells in this dossier.

cards.title: When You Spot Discomfort in a Negotiation, Give More Information, Not More Pressure
cards.hook: You just caught a fear flash on the other side of the table. Most people push harder. That is the wrong move every time.
cards.truth:
Fear in negotiation signals the other person does not have enough information to move forward safely.
• More pressure confirms the threat and locks them in place.
• More detail on the specific thing that triggered the fear opens them back up.
• The microexpression told you which topic to address — use it as a navigation tool, not a reason to press.
cards.principle: Voss: Tactical Empathy — Reading and Responding to Emotional State
cards.remember: Pressure on a scared face makes it worse. Information makes it better.
cards.theySee: A negotiator who pauses when they catch your expression and goes back to explain instead of pushing the next point.

signals.t: Wide eyes and raised brows appear for under a second right as a specific number is stated.
A nose wrinkle or upper lip lift appears briefly when a specific term in the proposal is mentioned.
A one-sided lip pull appears when you describe your qualifications or experience.
Brows drop and jaw sets when a previous decision or commitment is referenced.

steps.title: Name the shift in neutral terms
steps.desc: When you catch a signal, say: "I noticed something shifted when I mentioned that — let me give you more context on how we got there."

steps.title: Give more detail on the trigger topic
steps.desc: Go back to exactly what caused the expression. Add data, explain the reasoning, show your work. Do not move past it.

steps.title: Ask an open question and wait
steps.desc: After giving the detail, ask: "What would make this feel more workable from your side?" Then stop talking. Let them name the problem the expression already pointed to.

cards.script: "I noticed something shifted when I mentioned that number — let me give you more context on how we got there."
cards.counter:
If someone responds to your discomfort face with more information rather than pressure, they are reading you.
• They are navigating toward your concern — that is how you know they caught the signal.
• Before the meeting, decide which numbers and topics you can't afford to flash fear on.
• A skilled reader uses your micro-expressions as a map of where your room to move actually ends.
cards.insight: The read is only worth having if it changes what you do next. Most people catch the signal and then do exactly what they were going to do anyway — which means the read was just a curiosity, not a tool.
